plot: Second person, daily-life format: you join the 1898 Klondike gold rush; eleven chapters cover why go, the ton-of-goods rule, the Chilkoot climb, the Golden Stairs, food, boats, the Palm Sunday avalanche, White Pass, Soapy Smith, Dawson, and the last chapter is the mystery of 533 film reels found in Dawson's frozen ground in 1978.

beats.say: Spring, 1898. A man stands at the bottom of a frozen mountain. A police officer tells him to turn around, unless he can carry two thousand pounds over the top.
Name, and your supplies. Where is your ton of goods? No ton, no Canada.
A ton? That's the weight of a pickup truck! How am I supposed to carry that?
This is the Klondike gold rush. For the next few minutes, you are one of the people who went. Almost everyone wanted gold. Almost nobody knew the price.
You'll learn why the police made this rule, what a year of food looks like, and what happened on the mountain on Palm Sunday. And at the end, a very strange thing buried under a town in the snow.
Chapter one. Why would anyone leave home for this?
I lost my job. Banks are closing everywhere. And the papers say there's gold lying in the creeks!
It was real. In August of 1896, three men found gold in a creek near the Klondike River in Canada's Yukon. A year later, a steamship docked in Seattle with a ton of gold on board.
Did you hear that? A ton of gold! I'm quitting the farm today!
About a hundred thousand people set out. Clerks, farmers, teachers, even a few doctors. Only about thirty thousand ever reached the goldfields.
Chapter two. Why the ton?
But why so much? I only need a pan and a shovel, right?
There's no store at the end of this trail. The Yukon winter lasts about eight months. If you arrive without food, you starve.
The police were not being mean. In the winter before, hungry miners in Dawson had nearly run out of food. The rule was meant to save your life.
By 1898, a ton meant about a year of supplies. Hundreds of pounds of flour. Beans. Bacon. Dried fruit. Tools, a tent, a stove, boots, and warm clothes.
So that's my whole life in sacks. And I have to carry every pound myself?
Pretty much. And it cost you several hundred dollars before you even left Seattle. That was more than many workers earned in a year.
Chapter three. The mountain.
You land in the little town of Dyea, Alaska. Ahead of you is the Chilkoot Trail, about thirty-three miles of mud, rock, and ice.
Thirty-three miles? That's not so bad. I could walk that in two days.
If you were carrying nothing, maybe. But you aren't carrying nothing.
A strong person could carry about fifty or sixty pounds at a time. Two thousand pounds divided by sixty is more than thirty trips.
Thirty trips up the same mountain? I'd be walking a hundred miles just to move my stuff!
Think about it like this. Imagine carrying a full grocery cart from Walmart up a snowy hill. Now do it thirty more times, and don't drop the eggs.
That's exactly what people did. Up with a load, back down for the next. Day after day, for weeks.
Some people hired packers. Many were Tlingit men and women who knew the mountains well. They carried loads for pay, and it wasn't cheap.
Chapter four. The Golden Stairs.
The last stretch is called the Scales, because packers weighed loads there. Right after it, the mountain turns into a wall of ice and snow.
People chopped about fifteen hundred steps into the ice. Everybody climbed them in one long line, shoulder to shoulder, carrying their sacks.
I can't step out of line! If I stop, everyone behind me has to stop too!
And that's true. Step out of line, and you might wait hours to get back in. So people climbed, rested for a breath, and climbed again.
Some of the steps were just a few inches wide. A slip with a sixty pound sack on your back could send you tumbling.
My legs are shaking. My hands are numb. How many steps are left?
Nobody answered, because everyone was counting their own. One step, then a breath, then another step. That was the whole day.
At the top, more than three thousand five hundred feet up, the wind never stops. There, the police waited to check every single sack.
Count it. Flour, beans, bacon. Good. You may pass.
Chapter five. Where do you sleep and eat?
You sleep in a canvas tent, or under a sheet of cloth tied to a tree. When it's twenty degrees below zero, you pile everything you own on top of you.
So what do I eat all day? The same thing every night?
Pretty much. Beans, bacon, bread called bannock, and tea. Fresh food was almost impossible to find. That led to a sickness called scurvy.
Scurvy comes from not eating fresh fruits or vegetables. Your gums bleed and your legs ache. Some miners paid a fortune for a single potato.
One potato costs how much? That can't be right!
Chapter six. Building a boat.
After the pass, you reach Lake Bennett. And here's something you didn't expect. To get to Dawson, you have to build your own boat.
Build a boat? I've never built anything bigger than a birdhouse!
Thousands of people had never built a boat, and they built one anyway. They cut trees, sawed boards by hand, and waited through the winter for the ice to melt.
On one day in late May of 1898, the ice broke, and thousands of homemade boats floated away at once. Some were gorgeous. Some sank right away.
Then came the rapids, and about five hundred miles of river. Many boats flipped. Many people lost everything they carried.
Chapter seven. The worst day on the mountain.
Remember the Chilkoot? Back in April, before the boats, the weather turned. Days of heavy snow piled up on the slopes above the trail.
The guides say it's not safe. But if I turn back now, I lose a whole winter. I'll go.
Weather like that was nothing new on the Chilkoot. But with so many people on one narrow trail, a slide would find a crowd.
Some did turn back. Many didn't. On Sunday, April third, 1898, a huge wall of snow slid down the mountain onto the trail.
It buried dozens of people between Sheep Camp and the Scales. The park service says more than sixty may have died. It was the deadliest day of the whole gold rush.
The news flew down the trail. But many people just dug out their sacks and kept climbing. The gold was still waiting, they said.
Chapter eight. The other road.
Not everyone took the Chilkoot. Some took the White Pass, a trail that looked easier. It wasn't. It was narrow, muddy, and full of pack horses.
Horses were worked until they dropped. About three thousand died on that trail. Today people call it the Dead Horse Trail.
Chapter nine. A trap in town.
The nearest town was Skagway. And the man who ran it, in a way, was a crook named Soapy Smith.
Friend! Come play a little game. Easy money, I promise!
Soapy's gang ran fake shell games, fake telegraph offices, and fake help desks. Honest people lost their savings before they ever saw the mountain.
In July of 1898, a man named Frank Reid shot Soapy Smith dead on a Skagway wharf. Reid died of his wound, too, twelve days later.
Chapter ten. Dawson City.
If you survive all of that, you float into Dawson. Overnight it had become a town of about thirty thousand people, in the middle of nowhere.
There it is! Dawson! Now where's the gold? Where do I dig?
And here's the cruel part. By the time most stampeders arrived, the best creeks had already been claimed. Many people had climbed that mountain for nothing.
A few people did get rich. A lot more got rich selling them things. Most went home with less money than they started with.
The people who stayed in Dawson often did better than the diggers. A baker, a laundry worker, or a cook could earn real money from tired miners.
So all of that, the ice, the cold, the boat, for nothing?
Not for nothing. People remembered it for the rest of their lives. But now, here's the strange part I promised you.
Chapter eleven. The mystery under Dawson.
Dawson was a rich town, and rich people wanted entertainment. So around the nineteen tens, movies came to town. But Dawson was at the very end of the line.
Film reels came last, after every other city had seen them. And sending them back cost more than the films were worth.
So the town kept them. For years, the reels piled up. Then, around nineteen twenty-nine, they got rid of a huge pile of them.
Those films were made of nitrate, which can catch fire very easily. So some were burned, and others were dumped in an old swimming pool, and covered over.
Then, in nineteen seventy-eight, a worker was digging at a building site in Dawson. His machine scraped something hard under the frozen ground.
Hundreds of film reels. Five hundred and thirty-three of them, kept cold in the permafrost for almost fifty years.
Most of those movies had been lost everywhere else in the world. Inside the pile was even real film of the nineteen nineteen World Series.
So all those silent movies were lying under the town the whole time?
Yes. And that's the mystery that's still strange today. The thing that survived wasn't gold. It was a pile of trash that a town was too far away to throw out properly.
Some of those films have been saved and restored. People can watch them today, because a town at the end of the earth couldn't afford to ship them home.
So think about it honestly. Two thousand pounds, fifteen hundred icy steps, and a boat you built yourself. Would you have made it to Dawson?
Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more true history.

long.title: 2,000 Pounds or Go Home: The Klondike Law, 1898 🥶
long.description:
Would you have carried a ton of gear up the Chilkoot? Tell me in the comments.

In 1898 the Mounties would not let you into Canada without about 2,000 pounds of supplies. This is what the Klondike gold rush was really like: 1,500 ice steps, the Palm Sunday avalanche, homemade boats, and a strange pile of movie reels found frozen under Dawson City in 1978.
